Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA)

Source: R/pcoa.r
pcoa.Rd

Ordinates samples from their distances, for plotting beta diversity. Also known as classical or metric multidimensional scaling. Gives the same coordinates and eigenvalues as stats::cmdscale(), ape::pcoa(), and vegan::wcmdscale(), but computes only the first few axes, which takes far less time and memory for large datasets.

Usage

pcoa(dm, k = 3L, correction = "none", cpus = n_cpus())

Arguments

dm

A dist object, such as from beta_div() or bray(), or a symmetric numeric matrix of distances. Must not contain NAs or negative values.

k

The number of axes to compute. Default: 3. Reduced, with a warning, to the number of axes with positive eigenvalues, which is at most \(n - 1\) for \(n\) samples.

correction

How to deal with negative eigenvalues: 'none' (the default), 'lingoes', or 'cailliez'. See "Negative eigenvalue corrections" below.

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), will use all logical CPU cores.

Value

A numeric matrix with one row per sample and one column per axis, named "PCoA1", "PCoA2", etc., as described in "Ordination result" below. Its attributes are:

  • method: "pcoa".

  • eig: The eigenvalue of each axis: of Gower's centered matrix, so on the scale of sums of squares. pca()'s eig are variances, these divided by \(n - 1\); dbrda()'s are too when any distance is 4 or more.

  • prop: The proportion of the total variance that each axis explains, eig / trace.

  • trace: The total variance: the sum of all eigenvalues, including negative ones.

  • correction: "none", "lingoes", or "cailliez".

  • constant: The constant that the correction added, \(c_1\) or \(c_2\) below; 0 with correction = "none", or when the distances needed no correction.

With a correction, eig, prop, and trace are those of the corrected distances.

Details

Method

With \(A\) the matrix of squared distances and \(J = I - \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T\) the centering matrix, PCoA finds the eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) and unit eigenvectors \(u_i\) of \(B = -\frac{1}{2}JAJ\). Axis \(i\)'s coordinates are \(u_i\sqrt{\lambda_i}\).

cmdscale(), ape::pcoa(), and vegan::wcmdscale() build \(B\) in full (\(n \times n\)) and compute all \(n\) of its eigenvalues, which takes time proportional to \(n^3\). pcoa() finds only the largest k eigenvalues, by block Lanczos iteration with thick restarts. That only needs products of \(B\) with a few vectors at a time, which are computed in parallel straight from dm, without ever forming \(B\).

Proportion of variance

The total variance is \(trace(B) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i<j}d_{ij}^2\), the sum of all \(n\) eigenvalues. prop is each axis's eigenvalue divided by it: the same as ape::pcoa()'s Relative_eig and vegan's "Proportion Explained", the values that phyloseq::plot_ordination() shows on its axes.

Non-Euclidean distances, such as Bray-Curtis, can give negative eigenvalues. They still count towards the total, so prop can sum to more than 1 over the positive axes. Axes with eigenvalues that aren't positive have no real coordinates and are dropped with a warning, as cmdscale() does. So are axes with eigenvalues at rounding-error level, below sqrt(.Machine$double.eps) times the first one, as in vegan::wcmdscale().

Negative eigenvalue corrections

A correction adds a constant to the distances between different samples, the smallest that makes them Euclidean, so that no eigenvalue is negative (Gower & Legendre 1986; Legendre & Legendre 2012, sec. 9.3):

  • 'lingoes' (Lingoes 1971) adds \(2c_1\) to the squared distances: \(d'_{ij} = \sqrt{d_{ij}^2 + 2c_1}\), where \(c_1\) is the magnitude of \(B\)'s most negative eigenvalue. That adds \(c_1\) to every eigenvalue but the trivial 0 and leaves the eigenvectors unchanged, so the axes are those of correction = 'none', with coordinates \(u_i\sqrt{\lambda_i + c_1}\), and trace grows by \((n-1)c_1\). The axis whose eigenvalue was most negative gets eigenvalue 0.

  • 'cailliez' (Cailliez 1983) adds \(c_2\) to the distances: \(d'_{ij} = d_{ij} + c_2\), where \(c_2\) is the largest real eigenvalue of the \(2n \times 2n\) matrix \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 2B \\ -I & -4B_2\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), with \(B_2 = -\frac{1}{2}JDJ\) the centered matrix of the unsquared distances. The axes change, and are computed from \(d'\).

eig, prop, and trace are then those of the corrected distances, and prop sums to at most 1. They equal ape::pcoa()'s Corr_eig and Rel_corr_eig for the same correction, and vegan::wcmdscale(add = 'lingoes') or add = 'cailliez'; \(c_2\) is cmdscale(add = TRUE)'s ac.

Negative eigenvalues above \(-\sqrt{\epsilon}\, trace(B)\) (with \(\epsilon\) = .Machine$double.eps, so about \(-1.5 \times 10^{-8}\) of the total) count as rounding error: such distances, Euclidean ones for instance, get no correction. constant is then 0, and the coordinates, eig, prop, and trace are identical to those from correction = 'none'. (ape and vegan correct those tiny negative eigenvalues too, so they can add a tiny constant where pcoa() adds 0.)

With k = \(n - 1\), the axis whose eigenvalue the correction makes 0 is dropped without a warning.

When to use a correction

Non-Euclidean distances, such as Bray-Curtis or Jaccard, have negative eigenvalues, so the positive axes' prop can sum to more than 1. Most plots simply show the first few positive axes, which is fine when the negative eigenvalues are small next to the axes plotted. A correction makes every prop a share of a total of 1, at a price: both corrections inflate trace, and so shrink prop, more so for more samples. Which inflates it more depends on the data. 'lingoes' keeps the uncorrected axes and only changes their eigenvalues; 'cailliez' changes the axes too. Another remedy is to transform the distances: the square root of Bray-Curtis dissimilarities, for one, is Euclidean (Legendre & Legendre 2012).

How the corrections are computed

Neither the \(n \times n\) nor the \(2n \times 2n\) matrix is formed. \(c_1\) is the largest eigenvalue of \(-B\), from the same Lanczos solver. \(c_2\) is the largest \(c\) for which \(B + 2cB_2 + \frac{c^2}{2}I\) is singular (on vectors orthogonal to \(\mathbf{1}\)), found by a Rayleigh-Ritz iteration that needs only products of \(B\) and \(B_2\) with vectors, computed together from dm. That iteration can settle on a root that isn't the largest (as with some exactly symmetric designs), so \(c_2\) is checked: the corrected matrix's smallest eigenvalue, computed from a fresh start, must not be below \(-\sqrt{\epsilon}\, trace(B')\). If it is, its eigenvector restarts the iteration, for up to 10 rounds, after which there is a warning.

The smallest eigenvalues usually form a dense cluster, which Lanczos resolves slowly, so corrections take longer than correction = 'none'. For Bray-Curtis distances between 2,000 sparse samples, on one thread, 'none' took 0.4 seconds, 'lingoes' 5 seconds, and 'cailliez' 20 seconds; cmdscale(add = TRUE), which builds the \(2n \times 2n\) matrix, took 2 minutes. How much longer depends on how tightly the smallest eigenvalues cluster. Each pass over dm takes time proportional to \(n^2\), while cmdscale(add = TRUE) and ape::pcoa() take time proportional to \(n^3\).

Axis signs and reproducibility

An eigenvector's sign is arbitrary, so different software can return mirror images of the same axis. pcoa() flips each axis so that its largest coordinate in absolute value is positive. Results are identical from run to run and for any number of cpus.

k larger than \(n - 1\) (the most axes possible) is reduced to \(n - 1\).

Ordination result

Every ordination function (pcoa(), pca(), rpca(), dbrda(), capscale(), mds(), nmds(), isomap(), tsne(), umap(), and so ordination()) returns the same kind of object: a numeric matrix with one row per sample and one column per axis, so that it can go straight into plot() or a data frame. Rows are named after the samples, when the input has names. Columns are named after the method: "PCoA1", "PC1", "RPCA1", "dbRDA1" or "CAP1" (then "MDS1" for unconstrained axes), "MDS1", "NMDS1", "Isomap1", "TSNE1", "UMAP1", and so on.

Its attributes always begin with these three, in this order, each with one value per column:

  • method: The method's ID, e.g. "pcoa" or "nmds".

  • eig: Each axis's eigenvalue, on the method's own scale: pcoa() and isomap() give the eigenvalues of Gower's centered matrix (sums of squares); pca() and rpca() give variances, which are pcoa()'s divided by \(n - 1\) for \(n\) samples; and dbrda() and capscale() follow vegan, which also divides by \(n - 1\) when any distance is 4 or more. NA for mds(), nmds(), tsne(), and umap(), which have no eigenvalues.

  • prop: The proportion of the total variance (or inertia) that each axis explains. Unlike eig, it is comparable between methods, so use it to label axes. NA where it isn't defined.

Attributes particular to the method follow them. The matrix has class "ecodive_ord" (as well as "matrix"), only so that print() lists the other attributes by name rather than in full. Subsetting with [, or as.data.frame(), gives a plain matrix or data frame without them.

References

Cailliez, F. (1983). The analytical solution of the additive constant problem. Psychometrika, 48(2), 305-308. doi:10.1007/BF02294026

Gower, J. C. (1966). Some distance properties of latent root and vector methods used in multivariate analysis. Biometrika, 53(3-4), 325-338. doi:10.1093/biomet/53.3-4.325

Gower, J. C., & Legendre, P. (1986). Metric and Euclidean properties of dissimilarity coefficients. Journal of Classification, 3(1), 5-48. doi:10.1007/BF01896809

Legendre, P., & Legendre, L. (2012). Numerical Ecology (3rd English ed., sec. 9.3). Elsevier.

Lingoes, J. C. (1971). Some boundary conditions for a monotone analysis of symmetric matrices. Psychometrika, 36(2), 195-203. doi:10.1007/BF02291398

Wu, K., & Simon, H. (2000). Thick-restart Lanczos method for large symmetric eigenvalue problems. SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications, 22(2), 602-616. doi:10.1137/S0895479898334605

See also

pcoa_biplot(), pca(), dbrda(), nmds(), ordination(), beta_div(), stats::cmdscale()

Examples

    ord <- pcoa(bray(ex_counts))
    ord
#>             PCoA1       PCoA2        PCoA3
#> Saliva -0.3891250 -0.03721713  0.296748867
#> Gums   -0.3951099 -0.05550727 -0.293514268
#> Nose    0.3179676  0.53707433 -0.006811864
#> Stool   0.4662673 -0.44434993  0.003577264
#> 
#> pcoa: 4 samples, 3 axes; % of variance: 48.5, 38.0, 13.5
#> Attributes: method, eig, prop, trace, correction, constant

    # Percent of variance explained by each axis.
    round(100 * attr(ord, 'prop'), 1)
#> [1] 48.5 38.0 13.5

    # Same coordinates as cmdscale(), up to the sign of each axis.
    cmdscale(bray(ex_counts), k = 3)
#>              [,1]        [,2]         [,3]
#> Saliva -0.3891250  0.03721713  0.296748867
#> Gums   -0.3951099  0.05550727 -0.293514268
#> Nose    0.3179676 -0.53707433 -0.006811864
#> Stool   0.4662673  0.44434993  0.003577264

    plot(ord[, 1:2], asp = 1)


    # Unweighted UniFrac has negative eigenvalues here.
    d   <- unweighted_unifrac(ex_counts, tree = ex_tree)
    ord <- pcoa(d, correction = 'cailliez')
    attr(ord, 'constant')
#> [1] 0.0002072223
    round(100 * attr(ord, 'prop'), 1)
#> [1] 98.9  1.1
